cards.back: The ~1,000 years between the fall of Rome (ca. 400s CE) and the Renaissance (ca. 1400).
Old English epic poem about a hero who kills monsters; its treasure burials parallel Sutton Hoo.
Thin metal strips (cloisons) soldered to a surface form cells, filled with enamel, glass, or gems like garnet.
European style ca. 1000-1200, "Roman-like": thick walls, rounded arches, barrel vaults, heavy massing.
Container, often precious and ornate, that holds a saint's relics (body parts or belongings).
Sedes Sapientiae: Mary seated frontally with Christ on her lap; Mary is the throne, Christ is divine wisdom.
Decorating fabric by stitching colored thread onto it (Bayeux Tapestry: wool on linen).
Semicircular arch inherited from Rome; hallmark of Romanesque building.
Monastery room where monks copied and illuminated manuscripts by hand.
Continuous rounded-arch ceiling like a tunnel; heavy, needs thick walls, so few windows.
Religious journey to a holy site to see relics; drove construction of big Romanesque churches along the routes.
Abbot of Saint-Denis who rebuilt its choir ca. 1140-44, creating the first Gothic architecture to flood the church with divine light.
Arch that peaks at the top; pushes weight more downward, allowing taller, thinner walls. Gothic hallmark.
Vault framed by crossing stone ribs that carry the load, so panels between can be thin and light.
Exterior arch that braces upper walls from outside, so walls can be thin and full of windows.
Colored glass pieces held by lead strips forming images; a rose window is a large circular one with radiating tracery.
Ornamental stonework holding the glass in a window, forming intricate patterns.
"New light": Suger's term for colored divine light through stained glass, meant to lift the soul to God.
Small, precious objects in costly materials (gold, silver, enamel, gems) for royal or elite patrons.
Image of Mary mourning the dead Christ across her lap (Italian for "pity").
Painting on wet plaster (buon fresco) so pigment bonds into the wall as it dries; permanent.
Mathematical system where parallel lines (orthogonals) converge at a vanishing point to create depth on a flat surface.
Depth shown by making distant objects lighter, bluer, hazier, and less detailed.
Renaissance movement reviving classical Greek/Roman learning and celebrating human potential and the individual.
Wealthy Florentine banking family who ruled Florence and funded Donatello, Botticelli, Michelangelo.
Paint of pigment mixed with egg yolk; dries fast with crisp, matte color.
"Light-dark": strong contrast of light and shadow to model forms as 3-D.
Painting on dry plaster; paint sits on the surface and flakes over time (Last Supper).
"Smoky": Leonardo's soft, hazy blending of tones with no hard outlines.
Pigment mixed with oil (linseed); slow drying allows layered glazes, rich color, fine detail. Perfected in the North.
Image made by transferring ink from a prepared block or plate onto paper; reproducible many times.
Relief print: cut away wood around the lines, ink the raised surface, press onto paper.
Intaglio print: lines cut into a metal (copper) plate with a burin; ink fills grooves, pressed onto paper. Finer lines than woodcut.
